The Verification Frontier

Where (if anywhere) can we measure critical AI literacy?

Derek C. Briggs — SSM 2026 (working simulation)

2026-06-19

How to read this document. It is deliberately built to be audited, not trusted. Critical AI literacy is the ability to catch a plausible-but-wrong artifact you cannot verify at a glance — which is exactly the position you are in reading machine-generated code. So every modeling decision below is tagged [CHOICE], and Sections 4.2–4.3 check the math empirically so you are not relying on my algebra being correct. If a claim is load-bearing, it is stated as something you can falsify.

1 The question

An LLM held at a fixed prompt has its variability set by a dial (temperature); across the handful of frontier models that variability is being engineered toward zero. So the durable human variance is not in the model. We conjecture it lives in critical AI literacy (theta): the capacity to detect and repair an output that is wrong but plausible.

This document asks a measurement question, not a philosophical one:

Given a model with capability c and “seductiveness” s, how much information does a single task carry about a person’s theta? Equivalently: how many tasks would we need to measure theta reliably, and does that number grow or shrink as models improve?

2 The measurement model

One task = one Bernoulli outcome: did the final answer come out correct after the human–AI interaction? We model the success probability for a person with critical literacy theta as

\[ P(\text{success}\mid\theta) \;=\; \underbrace{c}_{\text{AI right unaided}} \;+\;(1-c)\,\underbrace{g(\theta)}_{\text{user catches \& fixes a wrong answer}}. \]

The two terms are the only two ways the final answer succeeds: either the AI was right on its own (probability c), or it fell short (probability 1-c) and the user over-rode it.

What “catch” means across domains. In a cheaply verifiable domain (code, math) “catching” is literal error-detection against an objective check. In a domain where verification is expensive or deferred (the dinner-party story) there is no such check at hand, so “catch” means appraisal: correctly judging that a fluent, joke-shaped output will actually fall flat for the audience, and not being captured by its polish. The criterion is then a deferred, social verdict (does the room laugh?) rather than a unit test. So read g(theta) as the probability the user correctly over-rides a plausible-but-inadequate answer — by detection where a check is cheap, by appraisal where it is not.

The catch-and-repair probability is a standard 2-parameter logistic (IRT) item:

\[ g(\theta) \;=\; \mathrm{logistic}\!\big(a\,(\theta - \delta(s))\big), \qquad \mathrm{logistic}(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} . \]

  • theta — the person’s critical literacy. [CHOICE] population distribution theta ~ N(0,1).
  • a — discrimination of the catch process. [CHOICE] a = 1.5.
  • delta(s) — difficulty of over-riding a plausible-but-inadequate answer, driven by model seductiveness s: how strongly surface fluency masks the (possibly deferred) verdict. More fluent duds are harder to over-ride, so delta increases in s. [CHOICE] linear map s in [0,1] -> delta in [-3, 3].
  • c — model capability, the probability the AI is right with no human intervention.

[CHOICE that you should attack] Here theta is operationalized narrowly as the ability to over-ride a plausible-but-inadequate answer — error-detection where verification is cheap, appraisal where it is not. Your blog series frames critical AI literacy more broadly (calibrated trust, knowing when to invoke AI, interrogating framing). This model captures one facet. Decide whether that facet is the right stand-in for the talk, or whether the construct needs additional items of a different kind.

A_DISC <- 1.5                 # [CHOICE] discrimination of the catch process
DELTA_MIN <- -3; DELTA_MAX <- 3   # [CHOICE] seductiveness -> catch-difficulty

logistic <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

# seductiveness s -> difficulty of catching a wrong answer
delta_of_s <- function(s) DELTA_MIN + (DELTA_MAX - DELTA_MIN) * s

# P(final answer correct | theta, c, s)
P_success <- function(theta, c, s) {
  g <- logistic(A_DISC * (theta - delta_of_s(s)))
  c + (1 - c) * g
}

2.1 Reading the parameters: an item characteristic curve

Plotting P(success | theta) against theta for a single item makes c and delta(s) concrete. c is the floor — the success rate of a person with no critical literacy, which rises with model capability. delta(s) is the location: the critical-literacy level at which success is halfway between the floor and 1. A more seductive item (higher s) has a larger delta(s) and shifts the curve right — harder to over-ride.

th <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 300)
cc <- 0.40                          # lower asymptote (model capability)
s1 <- 0.50; s2 <- 0.75              # two seductiveness levels
d1 <- delta_of_s(s1); d2 <- delta_of_s(s2)   # -> delta = 0 and 1.5
mid <- (cc + 1) / 2                 # halfway between floor and ceiling

plot(th, P_success(th, cc, s1), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#1f77b4", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = expression(paste("critical literacy  ", theta)),
     ylab = expression(paste("P(success | ", theta, ")")),
     main = "A hypothetical item characteristic curve")
lines(th, P_success(th, cc, s2), lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = "#d62728")

abline(h = cc, col = "gray55", lty = 3); abline(h = 1, col = "gray80", lty = 3)
text(-3.9, cc - 0.06, paste0("c = ", cc, "  (floor = model capability)"),
     pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = "gray30")

# delta(s) = theta where the curve passes the halfway point
segments(d1, 0, d1, mid, col = "#1f77b4", lty = 3)
points(d1, mid, pch = 19, col = "#1f77b4"); points(d2, mid, pch = 19, col = "#d62728")
text(d1, mid + 0.05, expression(delta(s)), col = "#1f77b4", pos = 2, cex = 1.0)
arrows(d1 + 0.1, 0.27, d2 - 0.1, 0.27, length = 0.08, col = "#d62728")
text(d2 + 0.1, 0.27, "more seductive", col = "#d62728", pos = 4, cex = 0.78)

legend("bottomright", bty = "n", cex = 0.85, lwd = 3, lty = c(1, 2),
       col = c("#1f77b4", "#d62728"),
       legend = c(paste0("s = ", s1, "  (delta = ", d1, ")"),
                  paste0("s = ", s2, "  (delta = ", d2, ")")))

2.2 Two domains: where capability can and cannot rise

The single most important refinement: c does not mean the same thing in every domain. The axis that matters is not a clean verifiable/unverifiable binary but the cost and latency of verification — how cheaply, quickly, and objectively the quality of an output can be checked. Write v in [0,1] for the cheapness of verification:

  • Cheaply verifiable (v = 1: code compiles, the theorem checks, the arithmetic ties out). An objective signal is available at once, so training can push capability close to 1. As c -> ~0.96 the opportunity term (1-c) -> 0, and by Check 3 the information about theta collapses. Critical literacy decays to “did you bother to run the test.”
  • Expensively / deferredly verifiable (v = 0: is this joke funny for my dinner party? is this framing wise? is this prose any good?). A verifier still exists — the room laughs or it doesn’t — but it is deferred, noisy, and audience-specific. Two consequences: (i) training cannot cleanly optimize against so sparse and after-the-fact a signal, so capability plateaus below 1 at c_cap — the model floor-raises fluency, not quality; and (ii) that same deferred verdict is the only scoring key for the human’s judgment, so critical literacy here is appraisal (seeing past fluency to anticipate the verdict) and remains the main thing between the user and a confident, plausible dud.

(Genuinely unverifiable output — pure preference with no convergent verdict even in principle — would have no scoring key at all, so critical literacy there would be unmeasurable, not merely expensive to measure. The interesting, measurable zone is real-quality-but-expensively-verified.)

We trace one model-progress path per domain. Generation g in [0,1] runs early -> frontier. Capability rises to a domain-dependent ceiling; seductiveness rises with fluency, shared across domains (a deliberate simplification — see caveats). The two roads start at the same early model and fork only because cheaply-verifiable capability can keep climbing while expensively-verifiable capability cannot.

C0     <- 0.50   # [CHOICE] early capability, both domains
C_CEIL <- 0.96   # [CHOICE] verifiable capability ceiling (objective signal -> ~1)
C_CAP  <- 0.55   # [CHOICE] unverifiable capability ceiling (no signal -> plateau)
S0     <- 0.45   # [CHOICE] early seductiveness
S_MAX  <- 0.62   # [CHOICE] frontier seductiveness (fluency rises with scale)

cmax_of_v <- function(v) C_CAP + (C_CEIL - C_CAP) * v   # capability ceiling by domain
c_traj <- function(g, v) C0 + (cmax_of_v(v) - C0) * g   # capability over generations
s_traj <- function(g)    S0 + (S_MAX - S0) * g          # seductiveness over generations

3 Why this model encodes the thesis (claims to verify)

These are predictions you can check against the code, not assertions to accept:

  1. Capability erases the construct. As c -> 1, P -> 1 for every theta, so the curve flattens and information about theta must go to 0. A strong model on a checkable task leaves nothing to measure.
  2. A verification frontier exists. For a population centered at theta = 0, a task is most informative when the catch-difficulty is matched to the population, delta(s) ~ 0, i.e. at an intermediate seductiveness. Too-easy errors (everyone catches) and too-hard errors (nobody catches) are both uninformative.

4 Fisher information: the per-task “measurement value”

For a single Bernoulli item with success probability P(theta), the Fisher information a response carries about theta is

\[ I(\theta) \;=\; \frac{\big(P'(\theta)\big)^2}{P(\theta)\,\big(1-P(\theta)\big)}, \qquad P'(\theta)=\frac{dP}{d\theta}. \]

Differentiating our P:

\[ P'(\theta) = (1-c)\,a\,g(\theta)\big(1-g(\theta)\big). \]

We report the population-expected information \(\mathrm{E}_\theta[\,I(\theta)\,]\) over theta ~ N(0,1): how much one task tells us about a randomly drawn person — i.e. the per-item value of the task as a measurement instrument.

# grid quadrature for theta ~ N(0,1)
THETA <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)
W <- dnorm(THETA); W <- W / sum(W)         # normalized N(0,1) weights

# analytic dP/dtheta
dP_dtheta <- function(theta, c, s) {
  g <- logistic(A_DISC * (theta - delta_of_s(s)))
  (1 - c) * A_DISC * g * (1 - g)
}

# Fisher information at a single theta
info_point <- function(theta, c, s) {
  P  <- P_success(theta, c, s)
  dP <- dP_dtheta(theta, c, s)
  denom <- pmax(P * (1 - P), 1e-9)
  dP^2 / denom
}

# population-expected information for one task
expected_information <- function(c, s) sum(W * info_point(THETA, c, s))

4.1 Check 1 — is dP/dtheta actually the derivative of P?

Before trusting the information formula, verify the analytic derivative against a finite-difference approximation. If my calculus is wrong, this fails loudly.

set.seed(1)
eps <- 1e-6
ok <- TRUE
for (i in 1:200) {
  th <- runif(1, -3, 3); c <- runif(1, .1, .95); s <- runif(1, .05, .95)
  num <- (P_success(th + eps, c, s) - P_success(th - eps, c, s)) / (2 * eps)
  ana <- dP_dtheta(th, c, s)
  if (abs(num - ana) > 1e-5) ok <- FALSE
}
stopifnot(ok)
cat("PASS: analytic dP/dtheta matches finite differences.\n")
## PASS: analytic dP/dtheta matches finite differences.

4.2 Check 2 — is the Fisher-information formula right?

The Fisher information equals the variance of the score \(\partial_\theta \log P(Y\mid\theta)\). For a Bernoulli outcome the score is \((Y-P)\,P' / [P(1-P)]\). We simulate outcomes at a fixed theta and confirm the empirical score variance matches info_point().

mc_information <- function(theta, c, s, n = 2e6) {
  P  <- P_success(theta, c, s)
  dP <- dP_dtheta(theta, c, s)
  Y  <- rbinom(n, 1, P)
  score <- (Y - P) * dP / (P * (1 - P))   # d/dtheta log-likelihood
  var(score)
}
set.seed(7)
for (case in list(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.4), c(0.6, 0.9, 0.55), c(-0.5, 0.7, 0.3))) {
  th <- case[1]; c <- case[2]; s <- case[3]
  cat(sprintf("theta=%+.1f c=%.2f s=%.2f  analytic=%.4f  monte-carlo=%.4f\n",
              th, c, s, info_point(th, c, s), mc_information(th, c, s)))
}
## theta=+0.3 c=0.50 s=0.40  analytic=0.1628  monte-carlo=0.1627
## theta=+0.6 c=0.90 s=0.55  analytic=0.0340  monte-carlo=0.0341
## theta=-0.5 c=0.70 s=0.30  analytic=0.1041  monte-carlo=0.1042

The Monte-Carlo column should track the analytic column to ~2 decimals. If it does, the per-task information function is trustworthy.

4.3 Check 3 — does information collapse as c -> 1? (Claim 1)

sapply(c(0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999),
       function(c) expected_information(c, s = 0.5))
## [1] 0.2024030024 0.0957198694 0.0207277451 0.0019963680 0.0001989109

These should march monotonically toward 0 — confirming that a more capable model on a fixed task carries less information about critical literacy.

5 Panel A: where the trait is measurable

cs <- seq(0.05, 0.98, length.out = 120)
ss <- seq(0.02, 0.98, length.out = 120)
INFO <- outer(cs, ss, Vectorize(expected_information))   # rows=c, cols=s

# verification-frontier ridge: best s for each c
ridge_s <- ss[apply(INFO, 1, which.max)]

# two roads across the same map, forked by verifiability
GEN <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 6)                 # early -> frontier
ver_c <- c_traj(GEN, 1); ver_s <- s_traj(GEN)    # verifiable domain (v=1)
unv_c <- c_traj(GEN, 0); unv_s <- s_traj(GEN)    # unverifiable domain (v=0)

filled.contour(
  x = cs, y = ss, z = INFO, color.palette = function(n) hcl.colors(n, "viridis"),
  xlab = "model capability  c  (P right unaided)",
  ylab = "model seductiveness  s  (subtlety of errors)",
  main = "A. Two roads across the same map",
  key.title = title(main = "info", cex.main = 0.8),
  plot.axes = {
    axis(1); axis(2)
    lines(cs, ridge_s, col = "white", lwd = 2, lty = 2)           # verification frontier
    lines(ver_c, ver_s, col = "white", lwd = 2)
    points(ver_c, ver_s, pch = 21, bg = "#1f77b4", col = "white", cex = 1.1)
    lines(unv_c, unv_s, col = "white", lwd = 2)
    points(unv_c, unv_s, pch = 21, bg = "#d62728", col = "white", cex = 1.1)
    # mark the shared start and the two frontiers (short, interior labels)
    points(ver_c[1], ver_s[1], pch = 21, bg = "white", col = "black", cex = 1.3)
    legend("topleft", bty = "n", text.col = "white", cex = 0.8,
           legend = c("verification frontier (ridge)",
                      "verifiable road (stats / code)",
                      "unverifiable road (the joke)",
                      "shared early model"),
           lty = c(2, 1, 1, NA), pch = c(NA, 21, 21, 21), lwd = c(2, 2, 2, NA),
           col = "white", pt.bg = c(NA, "#1f77b4", "#d62728", "white"))
  })

White dashed line = the verification frontier (most-informative s per c); white solid line with red points = the model-progress path.

6 Panel B: the window narrows for verifiable tasks, not unverifiable ones

The info-vs-s curve is a function of c and s only — the surface is the same map for any domain. What v controls is which c a domain can reach. So we slice the map at the three capabilities the two roads actually occupy: the shared early model, the unverifiable frontier (C_CAP), and the verifiable frontier (C_CEIL).

infoB_early <- sapply(ss, function(s) expected_information(C0,     s))  # 0.50, both domains, early
infoB_unv   <- sapply(ss, function(s) expected_information(C_CAP,  s))  # 0.55, unverifiable frontier
infoB_ver   <- sapply(ss, function(s) expected_information(C_CEIL, s))  # 0.96, verifiable frontier

plot(ss, infoB_early, type = "l", lwd = 2.4, col = "#444444",
     ylim = c(0, max(infoB_early)),
     xlab = "model seductiveness  s",
     ylab = "info about critical literacy (per task)",
     main = "B. The window narrows for verifiable tasks, not unverifiable ones")
lines(ss, infoB_unv, lwd = 2.8, col = "#d62728")
lines(ss, infoB_ver, lwd = 2.8, col = "#1f77b4")
legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 1.0, lwd = 2.4,
       legend = c("c = 0.50", "c = 0.55", "c = 0.96"),
       col = c("#444444", "#d62728", "#1f77b4"))

The unverifiable frontier (red) sits almost on top of the early model (grey): in deferredly-verified domains the measurement window barely narrows. Only the verifiable frontier (blue) collapses — the same v-contrast as Panel A, now sliced along s.

7 Panel C: is AI literacy a transient construct?

Translate information into a tangible cost. For a trait with variance 1, total information I_tot gives reliability rho = I_tot / (I_tot + 1), so reaching rho = 0.80 needs I_tot = 4. The number of trap-items required is 4 / E[info per item].

RHO <- 0.80
I_NEED <- RHO / (1 - RHO)                     # = 4
items_for_reliability <- function(c, s) {
  e <- expected_information(c, s)
  if (e <= 1e-6) Inf else I_NEED / e
}

ver_info <- mapply(expected_information, ver_c, ver_s)   # verifiable road
unv_info <- mapply(expected_information, unv_c, unv_s)   # unverifiable road
gens <- seq_along(GEN)

plot(gens, unv_info, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#d62728", lwd = 2.3,
     ylim = c(0, max(unv_info, ver_info)),
     xlab = "model generation  (early -> frontier)",
     ylab = "info per task about critical literacy",
     main = "C. Verifiable literacy decays; unverifiable persists")
lines(gens, ver_info, type = "b", pch = 17, col = "#1f77b4", lwd = 2.3)
legend("right", c("unverifiable (the joke)", "verifiable (stats / code)"),
       col = c("#d62728", "#1f77b4"), pch = c(19, 17), lwd = 2.3, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)

8 An item-bank version: seductiveness vs. item difficulty

The model so far uses a single over-ride difficulty per generation, delta_of_s(s) — a one-item caricature. A real design has a bank of prompts whose errors vary in how seductive they are. So we promote delta_of_s(s) from “the difficulty” to the mean of an item-difficulty distribution, and draw a bank around it:

\[ \delta_i \sim \mathrm{N}\big(\delta(s),\; \sigma_\delta\big), \qquad i = 1, \dots, N_\mathrm{items} . \]

Capability c stays fixed per generation (your call this round). A key consequence: because seductiveness s is shared across the two domains, they draw from the same difficulty bank and differ only in the model that scores it (c = C_CAP vs c = C_CEIL).

SIGMA_DELTA <- 1.0     # [CHOICE] spread of item difficulties (logits) around the mean
N_ITEMS     <- 200     # [CHOICE] prompts in the bank
BANK_SEED   <- 2026

# per-item info as a function of difficulty delta DIRECTLY (theta ~ N(0,1))
info_point_delta <- function(theta, c, delta) {
  g  <- logistic(A_DISC * (theta - delta))
  P  <- c + (1 - c) * g
  dP <- (1 - c) * A_DISC * g * (1 - g)
  dP^2 / pmax(P * (1 - P), 1e-9)
}
ei_delta <- function(c, delta) sum(W * info_point_delta(THETA, c, delta))

# consistency: the representative-item model is just the single-item case
stopifnot(abs(ei_delta(0.55, delta_of_s(0.62)) -
              expected_information(0.55, 0.62)) < 1e-9)
cat("PASS: ei_delta reproduces the representative-item information.\n")
## PASS: ei_delta reproduces the representative-item information.
# exact bank expectation: average per-item info over delta ~ N(delta_of_s(s), sigma)
DELTA_GRID <- seq(-7, 7, length.out = 281)
bank_info_exact <- function(c, s, sigma = SIGMA_DELTA) {
  wd <- dnorm(DELTA_GRID, delta_of_s(s), sigma); wd <- wd / sum(wd)
  sum(wd * sapply(DELTA_GRID, function(d) ei_delta(c, d)))
}

# a concrete RANDOM bank of N_ITEMS prompts
draw_bank <- function(c, s, sigma = SIGMA_DELTA, n = N_ITEMS, seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  delta_i <- rnorm(n, delta_of_s(s), sigma)
  list(delta = delta_i,
       info  = sapply(delta_i, function(d) ei_delta(c, d)))
}

8.1 Same bank, two capabilities

The same trap-items are highly informative scored through a weak model and nearly useless scored through a strong one — the divergence is entirely in the lower asymptote, not the difficulties.

s_front <- S_MAX                              # shared frontier seductiveness (= 0.62)
set.seed(BANK_SEED)
delta_i  <- rnorm(N_ITEMS, delta_of_s(s_front), SIGMA_DELTA)
info_unv <- sapply(delta_i, function(d) ei_delta(C_CAP,  d))   # c = 0.55 (unverifiable)
info_ver <- sapply(delta_i, function(d) ei_delta(C_CEIL, d))   # c = 0.96 (verifiable)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
hist(delta_i, breaks = 20, col = "gray70", border = "white",
     main = "Shared item bank", xlab = "delta_i  (logits; 0 = population mean)")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
boxplot(list(unverifiable = info_unv, verifiable = info_ver),
        col = c("#d62728", "#1f77b4"), ylab = "per-item info about theta",
        main = "Same bank, two models")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat(sprintf("random bank  : unverifiable mean=%.4f (items=%.0f) | verifiable mean=%.4f (items=%.0f)\n",
            mean(info_unv), 4/mean(info_unv), mean(info_ver), 4/mean(info_ver)))
## random bank  : unverifiable mean=0.0739 (items=54) | verifiable mean=0.0053 (items=757)
cat(sprintf("exact bank   : unverifiable     =%.4f             | verifiable     =%.4f\n",
            bank_info_exact(C_CAP, s_front), bank_info_exact(C_CEIL, s_front)))
## exact bank   : unverifiable     =0.0734             | verifiable     =0.0052

8.2 The divergence survives a real bank

ver_info_bank <- sapply(seq_along(GEN), function(i) bank_info_exact(ver_c[i], ver_s[i]))
unv_info_bank <- sapply(seq_along(GEN), function(i) bank_info_exact(unv_c[i], unv_s[i]))

plot(gens, unv_info_bank, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#d62728", lwd = 2.3,
     ylim = c(0, max(unv_info_bank, unv_info)),
     xlab = "model generation  (early -> frontier)",
     ylab = "bank-average info per task",
     main = "C'. Item-bank version: the divergence survives")
lines(gens, ver_info_bank, type = "b", pch = 17, col = "#1f77b4", lwd = 2.3)
lines(gens, unv_info, lty = 3, col = "#d62728")     # representative-item, for comparison
lines(gens, ver_info, lty = 3, col = "#1f77b4")
legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       legend = c("unverifiable (bank)", "verifiable (bank)", "representative item (dotted)"),
       col = c("#d62728", "#1f77b4", "gray40"), pch = c(19, 17, NA),
       lty = c(1, 1, 3), lwd = 2)

Bank-average information is lower than the representative-item value (the bank includes off-target prompts), so items-needed rises modestly — the joke goes from ~50 to ~55, the verifiable frontier from ~719 to ~769 — but the verifiable-vs-unverifiable gap is unchanged.

8.3 Sampling variability of a random bank

Because the bank is drawn at random, the items-needed estimate has its own uncertainty. This is honest measurement bookkeeping — and a reminder that “50 items” is itself an estimate.

set.seed(BANK_SEED)
reps <- replicate(300, {
  d <- rnorm(N_ITEMS, delta_of_s(s_front), SIGMA_DELTA)
  4 / mean(sapply(d, function(x) ei_delta(C_CAP, x)))
})
cat(sprintf("Unverifiable frontier, items-needed across 300 random banks of %d prompts:\n  median=%.0f   90%% interval [%.0f, %.0f]\n",
            N_ITEMS, median(reps), quantile(reps, .05), quantile(reps, .95)))
## Unverifiable frontier, items-needed across 300 random banks of 200 prompts:
##   median=54   90% interval [52, 58]

Wider SIGMA_DELTA scatters prompts further from the informative region, lowering average information and raising items-needed: that is the design lever for how tightly the prompt bank should target the population. The “moving frontier” becomes concrete here — as s drifts up across generations, you must re-center delta_of_s(s) and re-cover the population, or the bank decays.

9 Honest caveats (the places to push)

  1. The verifiable/unverifiable split is now in the model (Section @ref(domains)), via a capability ceiling c_cap for unverifiable domains. The remaining simplification is that seductiveness s is shared across domains. A fuller model would also let verification suppress effective seductiveness in verifiable domains (you can catch any error if you run the check), which would push the verifiable road off the ridge even faster. The capability ceiling alone already produces the divergence, so I kept s shared to isolate one mechanism. Attack the ceilings: C_CAP = 0.55 is a guess — change it in the Section @ref(domains) chunk and re-knit to move the unverifiable plateau; the sensitivity() block below varies a and the seductiveness range.
  2. delta(s) linear, a constant, theta ~ N(0,1) are all conveniences. Re-run the sliders below to see whether conclusions survive.
  3. Independence and unidimensionality. Items are treated as conditionally independent given a single theta. If catching errors is multidimensional (domain priors vs. tool fluency — the Chollet confound), this overstates information.
  4. theta = over-riding a plausible-but-inadequate answer (detection where verification is cheap, appraisal where it is deferred). See the construct caveat in Section 2. Note the scoring-key dependence: measuring theta in an expensively-verified domain needs the deferred verdict (e.g. the audience) as a criterion — so “50 items” understates the real cost, and a domain with no convergent verdict at all would make theta unmeasurable, not just costly.
# Re-run the whole story under your own assumptions.
# NOTE: this temporarily sets the global parameters, then RESTORES them on exit,
# so calling it leaves no side effects (an earlier version leaked global state --
# see the lesson in the prose above).
sensitivity <- function(a = 1.5, dmin = -3, dmax = 3, rho = 0.80) {
  old <- list(A_DISC, DELTA_MIN, DELTA_MAX)
  on.exit({ A_DISC <<- old[[1]]; DELTA_MIN <<- old[[2]]; DELTA_MAX <<- old[[3]] })
  A_DISC <<- a; DELTA_MIN <<- dmin; DELTA_MAX <<- dmax
  data.frame(
    verifiable_frontier = (rho/(1-rho)) / expected_information(0.96, 0.62),
    unverifiable_frontier = (rho/(1-rho)) / expected_information(0.55, 0.62),
    shared_early = (rho/(1-rho)) / expected_information(0.50, 0.45)
  )
}
sensitivity()                       # defaults (delta -3..3, a=1.5)
##   verifiable_frontier unverifiable_frontier shared_early
## 1            718.5055              49.90846     30.22994
sensitivity(a = 1.0)                # less discriminating catch process
##   verifiable_frontier unverifiable_frontier shared_early
## 1            1304.687              89.34727     57.11708
sensitivity(dmin = -2, dmax = 2)    # narrower seductiveness range
##   verifiable_frontier unverifiable_frontier shared_early
## 1            613.6437              43.35545     30.50849

10 What to take to the talk

  • Two roads, one map. The same model progress that drives critical literacy off the measurable ridge in verifiable domains (code/stats) keeps it on the ridge in unverifiable ones (the joke) — because capability can climb toward 1 only where there is a ground-truth signal to climb. See the headline table for the trap-items each road needs.
  • The construct is most measurable exactly where the model can help least. Critical AI literacy is durable in domains where the AI cannot verify itself — judgment, taste, framing, wisdom — which is both why it matters and why it is hard to certify.
  • A live empirical question, not a settled one. Whether unverifiable-domain literacy truly persists, or eventually erodes as fluency outruns human detection (s past the catchable band), is the design that a future study would test. That is Chollet’s generalization frontier relocated onto the human.
